common_name: Royal Red Butterfly Bush (Deep Magenta-Red Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; deadhead spent flower spikes regularly to extend bloom and to limit self-seeding, since Buddleja davidii can naturalize in some regions.

directions: Royal Red is one of the older, most established butterfly bush cultivars, producing long, dense, conical flower spikes in an intense reddish-magenta-purple that reads as the deepest red available among widely grown butterfly bush colors, each with a small orange eye at the center of the individual florets. It blooms in heavy flushes from summer through fall on a large, vigorous, arching shrub that draws swallowtails, monarchs, fritillaries, and hummingbirds in significant numbers whenever it is in flower. In zone 9 it behaves as a woody perennial that dies back hard in winter and regrows vigorously each spring, so cut the entire plant back to about 12 inches in late winter to keep growth compact and maximize the coming season's flower production.

common_name: Pink Delight Butterfly Bush (Clear Pink Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; deadhead spent flower spikes regularly to extend bloom and limit self-seeding.

directions: Pink Delight is a classic, long-grown butterfly bush cultivar carrying long, dense, conical spikes of clear rose-pink flowers on a large, vigorous, arching shrub, one of the most reliable and widely available pink-flowered buddleja selections. The clean pink tone pairs easily with both cool and warm companion colors in a mixed border, and like other butterfly bush cultivars it draws swallowtails, monarchs, and hummingbirds heavily throughout its long summer-into-fall bloom season. In zone 9 it dies back hard over winter and should be cut to about 12 inches from the ground in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth for the coming season.

common_name: Nanho Purple Butterfly Bush (Compact Fine-Textured Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Nanho Purple's smaller mature size needs far less pruning to control than standard butterfly bush cultivars.

directions: Nanho Purple is a compact selection from the Nanho series of butterfly bush, bred for a smaller mature size and finer-textured, narrower gray-green leaves than standard Buddleja davidii cultivars, fitting more easily into a mixed border without becoming an overwhelming presence. Its slender purple flower spikes are produced in abundance from summer through fall, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds just as reliably as larger cultivars despite the reduced plant size. In zone 9 it dies back over winter and should be cut back hard, to about 12 inches, in late winter to keep its naturally more compact habit tidy and to maximize summer bloom.

common_name: Ice Chip Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile White Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth, the same care as its sibling Blue Chip.

directions: Ice Chip is the white-flowered counterpart to Blue Chip in the dwarf, sterile Lo and Behold butterfly bush series, staying under three feet tall and wide while producing a continuous supply of pure white flower spikes from summer through frost. Its low, mounding, sterile habit avoids the self-seeding concerns associated with larger Buddleja davidii cultivars, fitting containers, small borders, and foundation plantings where standard butterfly bush would quickly outgrow the space. Like its siblings in the series it draws butterflies and hummingbirds heavily despite its small size, tolerates heat and drought well once established, and needs only the same annual hard cutback in late winter to stay compact and floriferous.
sources: North Carolina State University JC Raulston Arboretum

common_name: Autumn Fire Sedum (Improved Deep Pink-to-Bronze Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; like Autumn Joy, Autumn Fire declines in rich, wet soil, so lean, well-drained conditions give the sturdiest, most upright stems.

directions: Autumn Fire is an improved sport of the classic Autumn Joy sedum, selected for sturdier, less floppy stems and larger, more richly colored flower heads that hold up better through the season, particularly in humid climates where the original Autumn Joy sometimes splays open. Succulent, blue-green foliage emerges in spring, builds into broccoli-like flower buds by midsummer, opens dusty pink in late summer, and deepens through rose and finally rust-bronze by fall, with the dried seedheads persisting attractively into winter. Extremely drought-tolerant once established thanks to its water-storing succulent tissue, it thrives in the same lean, sharply drained, full-sun conditions as its parent and should not be planted where regular irrigation keeps the soil consistently moist, which encourages weak, sprawling growth. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in spring.
